title: The Faintest Line
subtitle: A shift on the dye district railway
story: This city's dye district made colors for two hundred years. When the trade died, the railway beneath the district went dark, but the lichen emerged: orange and grey-green, creeping across the old tile. Your biotechnology company scrapes the lichen off the tunnel walls and sells it on today's boutique pigment market. You have two jobs today. First, work out which gene in the lichen's genome controls pigment abundance. Then, find somewhere new to grow the lichen: places on the network that no train has stopped at in decades. Ride the lines. Keep your eyes open.

done.title: The gene is discovered!
done.body: You've named the key gene, excellent! Nine seasons wasted, but hopefully our company can breed for color again, now that it knows which gene to select on. Now, can you find the locations of new stations in which to grow lichen?

escapeDone.title: There is a great deal of wall down there!
escapeDone.body: Two platforms that were on no map are on the record, fixed off nothing but five route cards laid over one survey sheet, and the dark platforms you ran through on the way. Great job!

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the reference pair
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 1 · pairwise correlation. ANSWER XAN_4574 (|r| 0.832 vs 0.079 for the runner-up, 10.5x). The probe is deliberately a SATELLITE pair — probing inside the pigment module would return XAN_1192 and spoil the boss. Correct index 2.

question.prompt:
Your company keeps one gene in mind as a reference: XAN_4418. Its behaviour is well understood.

The sheets under the clip on this desk are the gene expression records from the whole lichen crop: two hundred samples, twenty-four genes, one expression level reading for each.

Which gene is most similar to XAN_4418 across the samples?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: XAN_4574 tracks the reference gene XAN_4418, |r| 0.83.
wrong: Correlate every other gene's expression against XAN_4418's across all two hundred samples, then rank by the size of the correlation — its sign does not matter here, only its magnitude.

One pair stands well clear of the rest: the winner is above 0.8 while every other gene falls below 0.1. If your answer sits somewhere in that crowd below 0.1, you have picked something out of the noise.
Check you correlated against XAN_4418 itself. The strongest pair anywhere in this dataset does not involve XAN_4418 at all, and two of the options belong to it.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the control gene
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 2 · threshold + one-vs-all. ANSWER XAN_6246, the sole isolate at |r|>0.75 (its strongest tie to anything is 0.103). THE THRESHOLD IS STATED IN THE PROMPT ON PURPOSE — the answer is stable only over |r| 0.15-0.7569; at 0.76 XAN_1815 and XAN_2781 also become isolates and the rung has three answers. NO HINT MAY SUGGEST A CUTOFF ABOVE 0.75. Correct index 0.

question.prompt:
Before your company will trust an assay it wants a control: a gene that is not correlated with any other gene in the dataset. Suppose two genes count as co-expressed here when the magnitude of their similarity exceeds 0.75.

Which gene has no co-expression partners at all?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: XAN_6246 is the control gene, with no partners at |r| > 0.75.
wrong: For each gene, count how many of the other twenty-three it is co-expressed with at a magnitude above 0.75. The control is the one whose count comes out at zero.
Several genes have exactly one partner, and one partner is not the same as none — if your answer has a single strong tie, it is a near miss rather than the control.

Hold the threshold at 0.75 as given. The control is isolated by a wide margin — its strongest tie to anything is barely above 0.1 — while several other genes sit just the other side of the line and would drift in and out if you moved it.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the standard protocol
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 3 · module + abundance. THE TAUGHT TRAP. ANSWER XAN_1815 (1434 units vs 245 for the next in module, 5.9x) — which has DEGREE 1. This is the method the works has re-seeded by for nine seasons while the colour thinned, and rung 4 is its correction. Correct index 5.

question.prompt: Your company grows each season's crop from a patch of the previous year's crop. The standard protocol says to choose the patch from this year's crop based in part on the following steps: (i) find the largest connected group of co-expressed genes (using the same 0.75 rule as before — start at any gene and follow correlations above 0.75 from gene to gene, so two genes belong to the same group if a chain of correlations links them), then (ii) find the gene within that group that has the highest average expression. In the current data set, which gene do those steps lead to?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: those steps lead to XAN_1815, the gene with the highest average expression in the largest co-expression group at ~1434 units.
wrong: Find the module first: the largest CONNECTED group. Start at any gene, follow every correlation above 0.75 to its partners, then follow theirs, until nothing new joins — that whole chain is one group, and two genes belong to it even if they are not directly correlated with each other. Only then compare average expression, and only within that group.

Stay inside the module. The highest-expressed genes in the whole dataset run above 5000 units and are not members of it; if your answer is one of those, you ranked across every gene instead of within the group.
Inside the module it is not close: the winner averages around 1400 units where the next one down is under 250.

puzzleQueue.label: The driving desk — the regulator
puzzleQueue.note: RUNG 4 · BOSS. module + network position. ANSWER XAN_1192 — the LOWEST-expressed gene in the dataset (71.5 units, rank 24 of 24), co-expressed with EVERY other member of its module (degree 7 vs 4 for the next). Decoy XAN_3514: loudest in the transcriptome at 5644 units, degree 3, and not even in the module. Correct index 3.

question.prompt: For the past nine seasons, each crop has had progressively less pigment than the previous ones. This year, your team is going to try a new strategy, based on the following steps: (i) find the largest connected group of co-expressed genes (using the same 0.75 rule as before — start at any gene and follow correlations above 0.75 from gene to gene, so two genes belong to the same group if a chain of correlations links them), then (ii) find the gene within that group that is connected to the highest number of other genes. In the current data set, which gene do those steps lead to?

feedback.correct: Correct — noted in your field notebook: those steps lead to XAN_1192, which regulates pigment production — the quietest gene in the whole record at ~72 units, yet connected to every other gene in its group.
wrong: Work inside the pigment module again, but rank its members by position rather than by size: for each one, count how many other members it is co-expressed with above 0.75.
The regulator is tied to every other member of its module and nothing else in the block comes close. Abundance will never find it — it is the quietest gene in the entire record.

If your answer is the loudest gene in the crop record, that is the bystander this whole assay exists to rule out: it runs at more than seventy times the regulator and is not even a member of the module.

debrief.title: How this world worked
debrief.intro: Everything in this scenario was one technique in costume: network analysis - describing a set of things by which of them are connected to which, rather than by how much each one carries. You did it twice over, on two networks that share nothing but this shift: one you built yourself out of correlations between gene expression readings, and one you could only observe by riding every line on the railway.

worldPlatePrompt: A wide establishing view inside a Victorian underground railway that stood derelict for a century and is now being worked again as a lichen farm. TIME-NEUTRAL soft even underground light, neither dawn nor dusk, no daylight in this frame. THE CROP IS THE ARCHITECTURE, AND THIS IS THE MOST IMPORTANT THING IN THE FRAME: the lichen grows ON THE FABRIC OF THE TUNNEL ITSELF, not in containers — thick living sheets of flat orange rosettes and swollen grey-green crusts spreading across the glazed wall tile, climbing the pilasters and furring the brick soffits of the arches overhead, so the walls themselves are visibly alive and shaggy with it. It is a crop growing on a building. Galvanised racking and plastic trays of cut crust stand about as the HARVEST TAKEN OFF THOSE WALLS — the product, never the source. Nothing is cultivated in a tray. THE FABRIC UNDER IT IS OLD AND DAMAGED: glazed brick and tile in ochre, saffron and dirty cream, much of it crazed, chipped or missing with the bedding mortar showing through; paint peeling in sheets off cast-iron columns; rust and water stains bleeding down; perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators; sooted segmental brick arches; granite platform edges worn hollow. A CREW WORKS HERE NOW, VISIBLY AND WELL: cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex strung along the arches, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, a kettle and enamel mugs on a plank shelf, a coat on a hook, and notices, work rotas, tally sheets and curling postcards tacked and taped to the tile with chalked marks and scratched tallies beside them. Repairs done with ingenuity — a propped timber, a patched panel, a hose run into a channel. TWO COLOUR TEMPERATURES, AND BOTH MUST BE STRONGLY PRESENT — this must NOT be a monochrome amber or sepia picture. WARM: pools of amber lamplight around the work-lamps and the crew's corner. COLD: everywhere the lamps do not reach, a distinct COLD BLUE-GREEN DAMP — wet black tile going blue in the shadow, green-black standing water, cold blue-green light down the tunnel mouths and in the depths of the arches, the chill of a place with a river behind the wall. The cold blue-green should occupy at least as much of the frame as the warm amber, and the two should meet in clear contrast rather than blending into brown. Damp air, faint haze, film grain. Photographic and beautiful. THE MOOD IS WARM, PURPOSEFUL AND CHARACTERFUL — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. It is emphatically NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin. Dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom for its own sake, no horror atmosphere of any kind. No large blank empty wall areas — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage or readable writing of any kind anywhere. No sepia monochrome, no uniform brown or orange cast over the whole image.
coverPrompt: A bold, graphic, MID-TO-HIGH-KEY square poster in flat vector-poster shapes. A single Victorian underground railway arch seen head-on and filling most of the frame, its opening a LARGE GLOWING field of warm amber lamplight — the brightest thing in the picture and the first thing the eye finds. Growing across that glowing arch, in strong flat silhouette, a bold band of LICHEN: fat round orange rosettes and a ragged grey-green crust spreading in from the arch's rim and over the tilework, deliberately oversized and simplified so it still reads at the size of a postage stamp. Two rails run out of the arch toward the viewer as two clean converging lines. The surround is a cool blue-green tile field, MID-TONE — clearly darker than the arch but never black. Three values only: bright amber, mid blue-green, and the orange crop. Big simple shapes, few of them, strong edges. NOT a dark or murky picture: no near-black fields, no deep shadow, no gloom, nothing dim, and no photographic haze — this is a printed poster, not a photograph of a tunnel. Square. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no logos.

sceneSpec.setting: the vast vaulted booking hall of a disused Victorian underground station, now the lichen works' traffic office and the topmost of its three stacked platforms, its ochre vault arching high overhead — the viewer is standing ON THE PLATFORM FACING THE LAMPBLACK TRAIN across its road, so that one road runs left-to-right across the view in front of them, with the platform's back wall behind them
sceneSpec.seam: the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it
sceneSpec.seamOccluder: a single cast-iron column, fluted, running floor to vault the full height of the frame

elements.desc: the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the left half of that one surface

out on the open platform floor between the viewer and the front of the locomotive, a little to the left of the viewer's line of sight: ONE round opening in the platform floor ringed by a single low iron railing, and inside it the top turns of a cast-iron spiral stair going DOWN, its worn handrail curving away into lamplight below. The stair and its opening are ONE object and nothing of it rises above the platform floor. It is the only stair in the station: EXACTLY ONE railed floor opening.
elements.label: The spiral stair down

elements.desc: in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND at the viewer's own feet, the platform's square worn granite edge with its white-painted line — and just beyond it the ballast and sleepers of the track bed, a single step down, with the two running rails lying on them roughly knee-deep below the platform surface: deep enough to take a train's wheels and no deeper. Those rails are the ONLY rails in the station: the same single pair runs on straight into the tunnel mouth at the left-hand end and straight into the buffer stops at the right-hand end, and the train stands on it.

dead ahead beyond that edge, this berth's single road: the sunken track bed and its ONE pair of running rails, its rails running away to the LEFT and ducking into its OWN brick-ringed arched TUNNEL MOUTH low at track level — the road between the train and that mouth completely CLEAR and unobstructed, so the train could run straight out of the station — while to the RIGHT, BEYOND the far end of the train, the same rails stop dead at heavy timber-and-iron BUFFER STOPS with a sand drag and a red lamp against a blind wall. These are ONE unbroken pair of rails running dead straight through the whole station and out at its end(s), and the train stands on that very pair, in line with them. Standing DOWN IN that bed, broadside to the viewer, a short heavy black iron works unit — flat soot-black sides, barred goods sections amidships — ONE vehicle, a single unbroken body, sitting square and level along the road with a driver's cab at the end nearer the viewer and its side doors slid open. ITS WHEELS SIT VISIBLY ON THOSE RAILS, squarely on the railheads and clearly in contact with them, and THE CAR'S FLOOR COMES UP EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE PLATFORM EDGE so its open doorways give straight out onto the platform at the viewer's own foot level, a single stride across with no step up or down and no drop in front of them. There is EXACTLY ONE tunnel mouth in the whole panorama, at the left-hand end of this single road, and no other tunnel, bore or arched opening anywhere; the right-hand end is the blind wall behind the buffer stops. THE TRACK GEOMETRY IS ONE STRAIGHT LINE: exactly ONE pair of running rails in the whole panorama, the very rails the train stands on, running dead straight along the platform and continuing straight into the tunnel mouth at the left-hand end, the mouth square on the end of those same rails and IN LINE with them. Only ONE platform, the one the viewer stands on; beyond the track is the plain far wall of the station, not a second platform. No second road, no siding, no crossover, no points, no other rails anywhere in the frame. At the right-hand end those SAME rails run straight into the buffer stops, which stand square ACROSS the ends of the two rails and in line with them, never off to one side of the track. The car's body follows those rails exactly: its wheels sit on the railheads along its whole length, so the car and the rails beneath it curve together as one.

sceneSpec.atmosphere: vast, cathedral-quiet, warm amber work-lamps against cold ochre tile and deep vault shadow, damp haze, film grain, sombre and grand. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake
sceneSpec.negatives: No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 1 tunnel mouth and 1 set of buffer stops in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. Each train sits SQUARE AND LEVEL along its own road, parallel to its rails — never nose-to-nose with another train, never wedged into a corner, never twisted, skewed or bent to show its far end, and never crossing another road. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. There is never a second set of rails running to the mouths beside or past the train, and the train is never parked on a stub of track that does not reach them. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs. authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the vast vaulted booking hall of a disused Victorian underground station, now the lichen works' traffic office and the topmost of its three stacked platforms, its ochre vault arching high overhead — the viewer is standing ON THE PLATFORM FACING THE LAMPBLACK TRAIN across its road, so that one road runs left-to-right across the view in front of them, with the platform's back wall behind them. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the left half of that one surface; just left of centre, out on the open platform floor between the viewer and the front of the locomotive, a little to the left of the viewer's line of sight: ONE round opening in the platform floor ringed by a single low iron railing, and inside it the top turns of a cast-iron spiral stair going DOWN, its worn handrail curving away into lamplight below. The stair and its opening are ONE object and nothing of it rises above the platform floor. It is the only stair in the station: EXACTLY ONE railed floor opening.; dead ahead in the centre, in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND at the viewer's own feet, the platform's square worn granite edge with its white-painted line — and just beyond it the ballast and sleepers of the track bed, a single step down, with the two running rails lying on them roughly knee-deep below the platform surface: deep enough to take a train's wheels and no deeper. Those rails are the ONLY rails in the station: the same single pair runs on straight into the tunnel mouth at the left-hand end and straight into the buffer stops at the right-hand end, and the train stands on it.; dead ahead in the centre, dead ahead beyond that edge, this berth's single road: the sunken track bed and its ONE pair of running rails, its rails running away to the LEFT and ducking into its OWN brick-ringed arched TUNNEL MOUTH low at track level — the road between the train and that mouth completely CLEAR and unobstructed, so the train could run straight out of the station — while to the RIGHT, BEYOND the far end of the train, the same rails stop dead at heavy timber-and-iron BUFFER STOPS with a sand drag and a red lamp against a blind wall. These are ONE unbroken pair of rails running dead straight through the whole station and out at its end(s), and the train stands on that very pair, in line with them. Standing DOWN IN that bed, broadside to the viewer, a short heavy black iron works unit — flat soot-black sides, barred goods sections amidships — ONE vehicle, a single unbroken body, sitting square and level along the road with a driver's cab at the end nearer the viewer and its side doors slid open. ITS WHEELS SIT VISIBLY ON THOSE RAILS, squarely on the railheads and clearly in contact with them, and THE CAR'S FLOOR COMES UP EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE PLATFORM EDGE so its open doorways give straight out onto the platform at the viewer's own foot level, a single stride across with no step up or down and no drop in front of them. There is EXACTLY ONE tunnel mouth in the whole panorama, at the left-hand end of this single road, and no other tunnel, bore or arched opening anywhere; the right-hand end is the blind wall behind the buffer stops. THE TRACK GEOMETRY IS ONE STRAIGHT LINE: exactly ONE pair of running rails in the whole panorama, the very rails the train stands on, running dead straight along the platform and continuing straight into the tunnel mouth at the left-hand end, the mouth square on the end of those same rails and IN LINE with them. Only ONE platform, the one the viewer stands on; beyond the track is the plain far wall of the station, not a second platform. No second road, no siding, no crossover, no points, no other rails anywhere in the frame. At the right-hand end those SAME rails run straight into the buffer stops, which stand square ACROSS the ends of the two rails and in line with them, never off to one side of the track. The car's body follows those rails exactly: its wheels sit on the railheads along its whole length, so the car and the rails beneath it curve together as one.; just right of centre, high in the ochre vault above the platform, long shafts of amber lamplight crossing the dark air beneath the ribs, thick with slow-drifting dust and damp haze; just right of centre, close beside the viewer, in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND an arm's length from the viewer, a galvanised bucket standing on the platform under a slow drip coming down out of the vault, half full of clear water, the tiles dark and wet around it, the drip falling steadily into the bucket, rings spreading across the water; to the right, standing well in from the right-hand edge of the frame, with a clear stretch of plain tiled wall between it and that edge — a heavy oak traffic-office desk out on the platform under a work-lamp, its sloped top carrying an open shift book and a folded linen survey sheet weighted flat, and standing on it a tall enamelled routing frame whose rows of blank enamel slots are all empty, a brass-handled lever beside them; on the far right, the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the right half of that one surface, joining its other half. vast, cathedral-quiet, warm amber work-lamps against cold ochre tile and deep vault shadow, damp haze, film grain, sombre and grand. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs. NOT two separate railways: there is no second pair of rails, no rails running in front of or behind the train other than the pair it stands on, no train floating over or beside its rails, and the buffer stops never stand off to the side of the track. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

sceneSpec.atmosphere: cramped, low, warm and domestic, saffron tile under a single string of work-lamps, damp haze, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake

It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 1 tunnel mouth and 1 set of buffer stops in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the grey berth at Cropping Yard, the loading end of the same broad cutting floor, where finished flats go up to the racks — the viewer is standing ON THE PLATFORM FACING THE LAMPBLACK TRAIN across its road, so that one road runs left-to-right across the view in front of them, with the platform's back wall behind them. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the left half of that one surface; to the left, the LEFT-HAND END of the station, low at track level, where the lampblack road ducks into its own arched tunnel mouth — each bore taking only its own road's single pair of rails, never shared, and the running road leading to it kept CLEAR: no barrier of any kind between a train and the mouth its line uses; to the left, a cast-iron spiral stair winding UP out of this platform through a round shaft in the roof, its worn handrail curving away into a pale glow above — it goes to this station's other platform, where the weld line stands; just left of centre, waist-high stacks of finished flats against the back wall, each a tray of dried orange crust, banded and chalk-marked and waiting for a car up to the racks; dead ahead in the centre, in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND at the viewer's own feet, the platform's square worn granite edge with its white-painted line — and just beyond it the ballast and sleepers of the track bed, a single step down, with the two running rails lying on them roughly knee-deep below the platform surface: deep enough to take a train's wheels and no deeper; dead ahead in the centre, dead ahead beyond that edge, this berth's single road: the sunken track bed and its ONE pair of running rails, its rails running away to BOTH sides and ducking into its OWN brick-ringed arched TUNNEL MOUTH at each — two separate bores for this road, one at either end of the station, low at track level, with the road CLEAR and unobstructed between the train and both of them: no buffer stop, gate, barrier or blockage of any kind on this road, which runs straight through. These are ONE unbroken pair of rails running dead straight through the whole station and out at its end(s), and the train stands on that very pair, in line with them. Standing DOWN IN that bed, broadside to the viewer, a short heavy black iron works unit — flat soot-black sides, barred goods sections amidships — ONE vehicle, a single unbroken body, sitting square and level along the road with a driver's cab at the end nearer the viewer and its side doors slid open. ITS WHEELS SIT VISIBLY ON THOSE RAILS, squarely on the railheads and clearly in contact with them, and THE CAR'S FLOOR COMES UP EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE PLATFORM EDGE so its open doorways give straight out onto the platform at the viewer's own foot level, a single stride across with no step up or down and no drop in front of them; just right of centre, a hard work-lamp on a bracket throwing a shaft of light across the loading end, thick with slow-drifting lichen dust kicked up off the flats; to the right, the RIGHT-HAND END of the station, low at track level, where the lampblack road ducks into its own arched tunnel mouth; on the far right, the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the right half of that one surface, joining its other half. broad, low and sooted, galvanised steel and black iron under hard work-lamps, dust haze, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 2 tunnel mouths in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. Each train sits SQUARE AND LEVEL along its own road, parallel to its rails — never nose-to-nose with another train, never wedged into a corner, never twisted, skewed or bent to show its far end, and never crossing another road. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. There is never a second set of rails running to the mouths beside or past the train, and the train is never parked on a stub of track that does not reach them. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

dead ahead beyond that edge, this berth's single road: the sunken track bed and its ONE pair of running rails, its rails running away to the LEFT and ducking into its OWN brick-ringed arched TUNNEL MOUTH low at track level — the road between the train and that mouth completely CLEAR and unobstructed, so the train could run straight out of the station — while to the RIGHT, BEYOND the far end of the train, the same rails stop dead at heavy timber-and-iron BUFFER STOPS with a sand drag and a red lamp against a blind wall. These are ONE unbroken pair of rails running dead straight through the whole station and out at its end(s), and the train stands on that very pair, in line with them. Standing DOWN IN that bed, broadside to the viewer, a short underground unit sheathed in copper gone bright green with patina, wet through — flat tunnel-profile sides beaded with water — ONE vehicle, a single unbroken body, sitting square and level along the road with a driver's cab at the end nearer the viewer and its side doors slid open. ITS WHEELS SIT VISIBLY ON THOSE RAILS, squarely on the railheads and clearly in contact with them, and THE CAR'S FLOOR COMES UP EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE PLATFORM EDGE so its open doorways give straight out onto the platform at the viewer's own foot level, a single stride across with no step up or down and no drop in front of them

sceneSpec.atmosphere: narrow, close and wet, dark tile gone green at the foot, one failing lamp string, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake
sceneSpec.negatives: No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 1 tunnel mouth and 1 set of buffer stops in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. Each train sits SQUARE AND LEVEL along its own road, parallel to its rails — never nose-to-nose with another train, never wedged into a corner, never twisted, skewed or bent to show its far end, and never crossing another road. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. There is never a second set of rails running to the mouths beside or past the train, and the train is never parked on a stub of track that does not reach them. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs.

sceneSpec.atmosphere: the coldest and lowest place in the world, pale grey tile and black standing water under warm lamps, heavy damp, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake
sceneSpec.negatives: No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 1 tunnel mouth and 1 set of buffer stops in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. Each train sits SQUARE AND LEVEL along its own road, parallel to its rails — never nose-to-nose with another train, never wedged into a corner, never twisted, skewed or bent to show its far end, and never crossing another road. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. There is never a second set of rails running to the mouths beside or past the train, and the train is never parked on a stub of track that does not reach them. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs. NOT two separate railways: there is no second pair of rails, no rails running in front of or behind the train other than the pair it stands on, no train floating over or beside its rails, and the buffer stops never stand off to the side of the track.

This is the ONLY stair in the whole panorama: EXACTLY ONE spiral stair and ONE round shaft, standing out on the open platform floor about a third of the way in from the left-hand edge of the frame and clear of the back wall. There is no second stair, no second shaft and no railed opening anywhere else in the frame, and none at either extreme edge.; dead ahead in the centre, in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND at the viewer's own feet, the platform's square worn granite edge with its white-painted line — and just beyond it the ballast and sleepers of the track bed, a single step down, with the two running rails lying on them roughly knee-deep below the platform surface: deep enough to take a train's wheels and no deeper. Those rails are the ONLY rails in the station: the same single pair runs on straight into the tunnel mouth at the left-hand end and straight into the buffer stops at the right-hand end, and the train stands on it.; dead ahead in the centre, dead ahead beyond that edge, this berth's single road: the sunken track bed and its ONE pair of running rails, its rails running away to the LEFT and ducking into its OWN brick-ringed arched TUNNEL MOUTH low at track level — the road between the train and that mouth completely CLEAR and unobstructed, so the train could run straight out of the station — while to the RIGHT, BEYOND the far end of the train, the same rails stop dead at heavy timber-and-iron BUFFER STOPS with a sand drag and a red lamp against a blind wall. These are ONE unbroken pair of rails running dead straight through the whole station and out at its end(s), and the train stands on that very pair, in line with them. Standing DOWN IN that bed, broadside to the viewer, a short heavy black iron works unit — flat soot-black sides, barred goods sections amidships — ONE vehicle, a single unbroken body, sitting square and level along the road with a driver's cab at the end nearer the viewer and its side doors slid open. ITS WHEELS SIT VISIBLY ON THOSE RAILS, squarely on the railheads and clearly in contact with them, and THE CAR'S FLOOR COMES UP EXACTLY LEVEL WITH THE PLATFORM EDGE so its open doorways give straight out onto the platform at the viewer's own foot level, a single stride across with no step up or down and no drop in front of them. THE TRACK GEOMETRY IS ONE STRAIGHT LINE: exactly ONE pair of running rails in the whole panorama, running dead straight along the platform and continuing straight into the tunnel mouth at the far end, the mouth square on the end of those same rails and IN LINE with them, never across them or at an angle to them. No second road, no siding, no crossover, no points, no other rails anywhere in the frame. There is EXACTLY ONE tunnel mouth in the whole panorama, at the left-hand end of this single road; the right-hand end is the blind wall behind the buffer stops. No other tunnel, bore or arched opening anywhere. At the right-hand end those SAME rails run straight into the buffer stops, which stand square ACROSS the ends of the two rails and in line with them, never off to one side of the track. The car's body follows those rails exactly: its wheels sit on the railheads along its whole length, so the car and the rails beneath it curve together as one.; just right of centre, close beside the viewer, in the IMMEDIATE FOREGROUND an arm's length from the viewer, a squat cast-iron soot-lamp standing OPEN on the platform, its wide shallow oil pan carrying a broad soft yellow flame a full hand high with NOTHING in front of it — no glass, no shield, no grille — and a thick black column of smoke lifting straight off the flame into a blackened tin hood held well clear above it on three iron legs, the hood and the tile above furred with collected lampblack — the flame and its smoke column large in frame and unobstructed, the nearest object in the view after the platform edge itself, a thin coil of smoke rising gently from the flame; to the right, standing well in from the right-hand edge of the frame, with a clear stretch of plain tiled wall between it and that edge — a single iron roof grating high above laying one hard bar of cold grey daylight down across the platform; on the far right, the platform's plain tiled back wall directly behind the viewer, uniform and unbroken, with no road, arch, doorway or opening in it, the right half of that one surface, joining its other half. the coldest and lowest place in the world, pale grey tile and one bar of cold grey daylight against warm lamps, heavy damp, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. No people, no lettering, captions, text, signage or readable writing of any kind, no station name, no daylight beyond that one bar through the roof grating, and no sky and no view out. EXACTLY ONE train and EXACTLY ONE road in this view — no second train anywhere, not behind the viewer, not at the frame edges, not down a tunnel. The train is ONE CONTINUOUS VEHICLE with a single unbroken body — never two separate vehicles, never two detached cab-boxes with a gap of floor between them, and never the same vehicle drawn twice. It is seen from the SIDE, standing straight and square along its road, and it is NOT bent, curved, twisted, skewed, splayed or wrapped round to bring its far end into view: only the flank facing the viewer needs to be visible, and the far end may simply run out of frame. COUNT THE TRACKWORK EXACTLY: this station has 1 road and 1 pair of running rails, ONE per train, and no others — no third track, no siding, no crossover, no points, no spare rails crossing the floor. Every road has its OWN bore, never shared, so there are EXACTLY 1 tunnel mouth and 1 set of buffer stops in this station, all of them on the viewer's LEFT and RIGHT and all in line with the rails that enter them. Each train sits SQUARE AND LEVEL along its own road, parallel to its rails — never nose-to-nose with another train, never wedged into a corner, never twisted, skewed or bent to show its far end, and never crossing another road. THE RAILS UNDER THE TRAIN ARE THE SAME RAILS THAT LEAVE THE STATION. One single unbroken pair of rails runs dead straight from one end of the station to the other, the train stands squarely on that pair, and each tunnel mouth sits directly in line with it — you could follow the railheads with your eye from under the train's wheels, along the bed, and straight in through the arch without a break, a bend, a kink or an offset. There is never a second set of rails running to the mouths beside or past the train, and the train is never parked on a stub of track that does not reach them. A BUFFER STOP MAY ONLY EVER STAND AT A BLIND END — beyond the far end of a train, on a road that dies there, against a wall. There is NEVER a buffer stop, gate, barrier, fence, hoarding or blockage of any kind BETWEEN a train and a tunnel mouth its own line runs into: every train must have a clear, unobstructed road out of the station. Nothing stands in the road but the train: no barrel, crate, bench or rack in the track bed. The image is SHARP, with no motion blur or streaking — everything is standing still. No blank empty wall areas. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs. NOT two separate railways: there is no second pair of rails, no rails running in front of or behind the train other than the pair it stands on, no train floating over or beside its rails, and the buffer stops never stand off to the side of the track. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the DRIVER'S CABIN at the head of the oldest unit on the network, in flaking oxblood-red on an underground works railway — the viewer is standing IN the cab itself at the controls, its walls wrapping right around them, the gangway door to the car behind at one end and the forward window over the driving desk at the other. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the left half of that one quiet stretch; to the left, the rear end of the cab: an offset gangway door in the rear bulkhead, glazed in its upper half, showing the dim passenger car behind, its wooden bench seats and string luggage racks just legible through the glass, stacked with harvested orange crust in shallow trays — a view through only; it is shut; just left of centre, a paint-spattered portable speaker wedged on the rear bulkhead shelf under a wrap of gaffer tape, its grille clearly visible and a charging lead trailing down the panelling — plainly the driver's own, and newer than everything around it; just left of centre, a small laminated route map tacked to the panelling just above the speaker shelf, held at its corners with gaffer tape, its plastic sheen catching the cab lamp — one single coloured route line with a few round station rings along it, too small to read from here; dead ahead in the centre, the cab's side door out to the platform, directly ahead of the viewer, its upper half a large panel of FROSTED ribbed glass — translucent and completely opaque to detail, so nothing whatever of what lies beyond it can be made out, only a soft even glow coming through; just right of centre, a worn wooden driving desk with a brass master controller, a brass brake handle polished bright by one hand, three round brass-bezelled gauges with plain unmarked dials, and a hinged writing-flap folded down at its left end carrying the works' assay sheets under a bulldog clip; just right of centre, a heavy brass driving lever on a short cast-iron pedestal at the outboard end of the driving desk, its worn handle standing upright in a slotted quadrant so it can be thrown forward or back, a small blank enamel plate at each end of the slot; to the right, the front end of the cab: its single large forward window above the desk, looking straight along the running rails down a PLAIN ROUND BRICK TUBE — evenly repeating brick rings running dead straight ahead, the twin rails converging away into the dark, lit by the unit's own headlamp and a receding string of small lamps dwindling to a point; no side arches, columns, alcoves, platforms or openings of any kind, just the one simple tube, the tunnel ring and running rails streaming steadily toward the viewer; on the far right, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the right half of that one quiet stretch, joining its other half. warm, worn and close, oxblood and varnished wood and dulled brass under one yellow cab lamp, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, no single-vanishing-point composition, and never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage, no readable writing of any kind, no destination names, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE opening in the cab shows anything beyond it moving — the forward window at the RIGHT. The side door dead ahead is FROSTED and no platform, station, tile, lamp or figure is visible through it. Behind the viewer is a SOLID BLIND WALL with no window, porthole or opening of any kind. There is NO door at the front of the cab — the front is a window only. The image is SHARP: no motion blur, no streaking, no smeared or doubled detail anywhere — everything in this picture is standing still, and any movement described is what the cinemagraph will add later, never something painted into the still. THE TRACKWAY IS NEVER FLOODED: wherever running rails appear they and their track bed are clear and usable, with no water standing over them, and there is no canal, waterway or navigable channel anywhere in the station — any water lies as shallow sheets or in a shallow drainage channel at the platform foot, never on the rails. The cab fittings are rigid: nothing slides, tips, rolls or drifts. No large blank empty wall areas anywhere — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs, no horror atmosphere. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the DRIVER'S CABIN at the head of a stripped goods unit in ochre-yellow on an underground works railway — the viewer is standing IN the cab itself at the controls, its walls wrapping right around them, the gangway door to the car behind at one end and the forward window over the driving desk at the other. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the left half of that one quiet stretch; to the left, the rear end of the cab: an offset gangway door in the rear bulkhead, glazed in its upper half, showing the open flatbed behind, seen through the glass — no seats, just stacked flats lashed down under canvas straps and the raw tunnel dark beyond the low drop gates — a view through only; it is shut; just left of centre, a battered yellow site radio bungeed to the bulkhead rail, its aerial bent and its grille clearly visible, a charging lead trailing — plainly the driver's own, and newer than everything around it; just left of centre, a small laminated route map tacked to the panelling just above the speaker shelf, held at its corners with gaffer tape, its plastic sheen catching the cab lamp — one single coloured route line with a few round station rings along it, too small to read from here; dead ahead in the centre, the cab's side door out to the platform, directly ahead of the viewer, its upper half a large panel of FROSTED ribbed glass — translucent and completely opaque to detail, so nothing whatever of what lies beyond it can be made out, only a soft even glow coming through; just right of centre, a bare iron driving desk with a heavy master controller, an oversized brake handle, two round gauges with plain unmarked dials, and a hinged writing-flap folded down at its left end carrying the works' assay sheets under a bulldog clip; just right of centre, a heavy brass driving lever on a short cast-iron pedestal at the outboard end of the driving desk, its worn handle standing upright in a slotted quadrant so it can be thrown forward or back, a small blank enamel plate at each end of the slot; to the right, the front end of the cab: its single large forward window above the desk, looking straight along the running rails down a PLAIN ROUND BRICK TUBE — evenly repeating brick rings running dead straight ahead, the twin rails converging away into the dark, lit by the unit's own headlamp and a receding string of small lamps dwindling to a point; no side arches, columns, alcoves, platforms or openings of any kind, just the one simple tube, the tunnel ring and running rails streaming steadily toward the viewer; on the far right, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the right half of that one quiet stretch, joining its other half. bare, hard-lit and industrial, ochre iron and scoured steel under a caged work-lamp, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. EXACTLY ONE opening in the cab shows anything beyond it moving — the forward window at the RIGHT. The side door dead ahead is FROSTED and no platform, station, tile, lamp or figure is visible through it. Behind the viewer is a SOLID BLIND WALL with no window, porthole or opening of any kind. Keep every object of interest well inboard. authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the DRIVER'S CABIN at the head of a copper-sheathed unit gone bright green with patina on an underground works railway — the viewer is standing IN the cab itself at the controls, its walls wrapping right around them, the gangway door to the car behind at one end and the forward window over the driving desk at the other. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the left half of that one quiet stretch; to the left, the rear end of the cab: an offset gangway door in the rear bulkhead, glazed in its upper half, showing the dim passenger car behind, its slatted seats and green-stained copper lining just legible through the glass, water running away under a grated floor — a view through only; it is shut; just left of centre, a green-cased waterproof speaker hung from a bulkhead hook by its wrist strap, beaded with water, its grille clearly visible and a charging lead trailing — plainly the driver's own, and newer than everything around it; just left of centre, a small laminated route map tacked to the panelling just above the speaker shelf, held at its corners with gaffer tape, its plastic sheen catching the cab lamp — one single coloured route line with a few round station rings along it, too small to read from here; dead ahead in the centre, the cab's side door out to the platform, directly ahead of the viewer, its upper half a large panel of FROSTED ribbed glass — translucent and completely opaque to detail, so nothing whatever of what lies beyond it can be made out, only a soft even glow coming through; just right of centre, a copper-topped driving desk gone green, a verdigrised master controller, a brake handle worn back to bare metal where it is gripped, three round gauges with plain unmarked dials beaded with damp, and a hinged writing-flap folded down at its left end carrying the works' assay sheets under a bulldog clip; just right of centre, a heavy brass driving lever on a short cast-iron pedestal at the outboard end of the driving desk, its worn handle standing upright in a slotted quadrant so it can be thrown forward or back, a small blank enamel plate at each end of the slot; to the right, the front end of the cab: its single large forward window above the desk, looking straight along the running rails down a PLAIN ROUND BRICK TUBE — evenly repeating brick rings running dead straight ahead, the twin rails converging away into the dark, lit by the unit's own headlamp and a receding string of small lamps dwindling to a point; no side arches, columns, alcoves, platforms or openings of any kind, just the one simple tube, the tunnel ring and running rails streaming steadily toward the viewer; on the far right, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the right half of that one quiet stretch, joining its other half. wet, green and echoing, patinated copper under a cold cab lamp, everything running, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, no single-vanishing-point composition, and never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage, no readable writing of any kind, no destination names, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE opening in the cab shows anything beyond it moving — the forward window at the RIGHT. The side door dead ahead is FROSTED and no platform, station, tile, lamp or figure is visible through it. Behind the viewer is a SOLID BLIND WALL with no window, porthole or opening of any kind. There is NO door at the front of the cab — the front is a window only. The image is SHARP: no motion blur, no streaking, no smeared or doubled detail anywhere — everything in this picture is standing still, and any movement described is what the cinemagraph will add later, never something painted into the still. THE TRACKWAY IS NEVER FLOODED: wherever running rails appear they and their track bed are clear and usable, with no water standing over them, and there is no canal, waterway or navigable channel anywhere in the station — any water lies as shallow sheets or in a shallow drainage channel at the platform foot, never on the rails. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs, no horror atmosphere. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.
