authoring.scenePrompt: This is a seamless 360-degree panorama from the DRIVER'S CABIN at the head of the works' heavy black iron unit, the only one never taken out of service on an underground works railway — the viewer is standing IN the cab itself at the controls, its walls wrapping right around them, the gangway door to the car behind at one end and the forward window over the driving desk at the other. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. It is NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, there is no single-vanishing-point composition, and it is never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. Directly behind the viewer, split across the extreme left and extreme right edges, is the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken: the far-left edge and the far-right edge are the two halves of this one surface and must match exactly in colour, texture, and lighting, joining into a single continuous, unbroken whole when the image wraps left to right. On the far left, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the left half of that one quiet stretch; to the left, the rear end of the cab: an offset gangway door in the rear bulkhead, glazed in its upper half, showing the cage-wagon behind, seen through the glass — no seats, heavy barred sides, a bare planked floor worn to a shine and the tunnel dark showing between the bars — a view through only; it is shut; just left of centre, a scuffed grey speaker jammed into a bulkhead bracket and held with cable ties, its grille clearly visible and a charging lead trailing — plainly the driver's own, and newer than everything around it; just left of centre, a small laminated route map tacked to the panelling just above the speaker shelf, held at its corners with gaffer tape, its plastic sheen catching the cab lamp — one single coloured route line with a few round station rings along it, too small to read from here; dead ahead in the centre, the cab's side door out to the platform, directly ahead of the viewer, its upper half a large panel of FROSTED ribbed glass — translucent and completely opaque to detail, so nothing whatever of what lies beyond it can be made out, only a soft even glow coming through; just right of centre, a soot-blackened iron driving desk with a massive master controller, a worn brake handle, two round gauges with plain unmarked dials, and a hinged writing-flap folded down at its left end carrying the works' assay sheets under a bulldog clip; just right of centre, a heavy brass driving lever on a short cast-iron pedestal at the outboard end of the driving desk, its worn handle standing upright in a slotted quadrant so it can be thrown forward or back, a small blank enamel plate at each end of the slot; to the right, the front end of the cab: its single large forward window above the desk, looking straight along the running rails down a PLAIN ROUND BRICK TUBE — evenly repeating brick rings running dead straight ahead, the twin rails converging away into the dark, lit by the unit's own headlamp and a receding string of small lamps dwindling to a point; no side arches, columns, alcoves, platforms or openings of any kind, just the one simple tube, the tunnel ring and running rails streaming steadily toward the viewer; on the far right, the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, the right half of that one quiet stretch, joining its other half. heavy, dark and grinding, soot-black iron under one caged bulb, deep shadow, film grain. A CENTURY OF DERELICTION, ACTIVELY WORKED IN: crazed and missing glazed tile with the bedding mortar showing through, paint peeling in sheets, long rust and water stains bleeding down the walls, perished cable looped on old porcelain insulators, chipped enamel, sooted brick, treads worn hollow. And over the top of all of it the crew who work here now — notices, tally sheets, work rotas and curling postcards tacked and taped up, chalked marks and scratched tallies on the tile, duckboards laid over the wet, cable ties and gaffer tape, cheap bright LED work-lamps on yellow flex, a kettle, a coat on a hook. Lived-in, cared for, and plainly somebody's workplace. Warm, purposeful and characterful — a magnificent run-down place that a good crew has taken on and made theirs. NOT eerie, NOT spooky, NOT creepy, NOT haunted, NOT menacing, NOT post-apocalyptic and NOT an abandoned ruin: dark and dirty in places, and still plainly and warmly worked in. No cobwebs, no gloom-for-its-own-sake. This is an EQUIRECTANGULAR 360 panorama, not a flat photograph: the walls wrap continuously right around the viewer with strong barrel curvature, the ceiling and floor bow across the frame, and any surface toward the left or right of the frame is at the viewer's SIDE, seen at a glancing angle rather than face-on. NOT a flat frontal elevation of one wall, no single-vanishing-point composition, and never a view of the room from outside it or from across it. No people, no lettering, no captions, no text, no signage, no readable writing of any kind, no destination names, no daylight. EXACTLY ONE opening in the cab shows anything beyond it moving — the forward window at the RIGHT. The side door dead ahead is FROSTED and no platform, station, tile, lamp or figure is visible through it. Behind the viewer is a SOLID BLIND WALL with no window, porthole or opening of any kind. There is NO door at the front of the cab — the front is a window only. The image is SHARP: no motion blur, no streaking, no smeared or doubled detail anywhere — everything in this picture is standing still, and any movement described is what the cinemagraph will add later, never something painted into the still. THE TRACKWAY IS NEVER FLOODED: wherever running rails appear they and their track bed are clear and usable, with no water standing over them, and there is no canal, waterway or navigable channel anywhere in the station — any water lies as shallow sheets or in a shallow drainage channel at the platform foot, never on the rails. The cab fittings are rigid: nothing slides, tips, rolls or drifts. No large blank empty wall areas anywhere — every surface carries the marks and clutter of a working place. Nothing eerie, spooky, creepy, haunted or menacing; no cobwebs, no horror atmosphere. Shot on a full-frame DSLR at 24mm, f/8, natural daylight, high dynamic range, realistic depth of field, fine natural film grain, true-to-life colour. EDGE DISCIPLINE: the leftmost 6% and the rightmost 6% of the image must contain nothing but the plain continuous backdrop named above — no object, structure, post, path, fence, building corner, vehicle or figure may appear, begin or end inside those two margins, and no cast shadow may fall across them. Keep every object of interest well inboard. THE GROUND IS ONE SURFACE: the ground at the extreme left edge and the ground at the extreme right edge are the SAME patch of ground seen from the same standing point. Its paving, texture, colour, wetness and the base of anything resting on it must continue unbroken and perfectly aligned across that join, at the same height and the same scale on both sides. Again: the extreme left and right edges must align perfectly into the blind side wall of the cab, the side that stands against the tunnel — a solid painted panel with no window, door or opening of any kind in it, uniform and unbroken, with no visible seam, join, or repetition.

ladderPlain.text: In the first puzzle you worked from lichen_expression, the crop's gene expression record: two hundred samples, twenty-four genes, one expression reading for each. You correlated every gene against the reference gene XAN_4418 across all two hundred samples and took the largest correlation by magnitude - XAN_4574, at 0.83, where every other gene in the dataset falls below 0.1. One pair of genes at a time, which is where a co-expression network starts.

In the second puzzle you turned those pairwise correlations into a network by fixing a cutoff: two genes count as co-expressed when the magnitude of their correlation is above 0.75. Counting partners under that rule, XAN_6246 has none at all - its strongest correlation with anything in the dataset is 0.103 - which is exactly what your company wanted in a control gene.

In the third puzzle you ran the standard protocol your company re-seeds the crop by. You found the largest connected group of co-expressed genes - following correlations above 0.75 from gene to gene, so two genes belong to the same group when a chain of correlations links them and not only when they are correlated directly - and then took the member of that group with the highest average expression: XAN_1815, at about 1,434 units, nearly six times the next gene inside the group. Both steps are exactly as written and the answer is exactly what they give. The last puzzle is about what the second step is measuring.

In the last puzzle you kept the same group of eight genes and changed only how you ranked its members: by position rather than by abundance, counting how many other members of the group each gene is co-expressed with above 0.75. That gives XAN_1192, which is co-expressed with all seven of the others where the next gene down reaches only four. XAN_1192 is the quietest gene in the whole record at about 72 units, last of twenty-four, so the abundance ranking of the third puzzle puts it at the bottom; and XAN_3514, the loudest gene in the record at about 5,644 units, is co-expressed with only three genes and is not a member of the group at all. Nine seasons of re-seeding from the most abundant gene in the group, rather than the most connected one, is why the colour kept thinning.

escapeBrief: To get out you filed the two stations that no record held. This second network was nothing you computed: its connections are the five lines, and the only way to observe one was to ride it, reading that line's stops off the route card taped up in the cab. Halliwell lies on the madder, woad and weld lines - three lines, as many as Ochre Steps, the grandest station on the network - and Cold Harbour lies on the verdigris and the lampblack, and the trains run through both without stopping, so neither is printed on any route card and neither is on the operator's survey sheet of live stations. You can only reach them by riding all five lines and catching the platform going past that nothing on paper accounts for, then reading its square off the grid in the margin of the sheet: E5 and I4, entered together into the Master Station List. That is the last puzzle performed instead of computed - a station's standing read off what connects to it rather than off any quantity - and the one station the record does treat as important turned out to be nothing more than where you went to file the report.
